description: Neck and Milliman (1994) spurred the scholarly dialog of spirituality in the organizational discourses by inquiring about two existential questions: ‘what relevance does spirituality hold in the workplace realm?’ and ‘how can work become a spiritual experience for the organizational workforce?’ They assert that work is envisaged to serve as one of the most powerful means to experience the divine in the world, i.e., to experience spirituality (Holland, 1989; Klenke, 2003; Neck & Milliman, 1994). Spirituality is the expression of an intimate relationship that one has with one’s spirit or animating force that influences how one engages oneself in this world (Fairholm, 1996). Fairholm (1996, p.11) maintains that spirit ‘must manifest itself in both our personal and professional lives’ and asserts that overlooking the spiritual selves of the organizational workforce is like ignoring the ‘essence of who we are’ (Fairholm, 1996, p.11). The spiritual quest underscores a dynamic process through which individuals transcend their limitations by experiencing a sense of interconnectedness and oneness, unleashing their true potential, realizing their sense of purpose, and with encompassing love, striving to help others in achieving this wisdom (Hawley & Hawley, 1993; Neck & Milliman, 1994; Vaughan, 1989). In the realm of workspace, when one's inner self connects with one’s work, both seem to be limitless ‘because it challenges the limits of being and stretches for the... spiritual horizon’ (Fox, 1994.p.82). Thus, the highest level of work is spiritual (Burack, 1999). Spirituality at the workplace has unfolded because of people’s pursuit of greater meaning in the realm of work and experiencing a sense of togetherness (Bhindi & Duignan, 1997; Klenke, 2003). First, researchers in this cluster attempted to critically analyze the complex SpiritualityReligion dichotomy. Bhindi and Duignan (1997), Cacioppe (2000a), Bierly et al. (2000), and Klenke (2003) perspicuously distinguished between spirituality and religion by alleging that organized formal religion is rigid and has an outward orientation through dependency on scriptures, rituals, and traditions while spirituality is turning inward into oneself, knowing oneself and embracing universal values. Spirituality is more eclectic and goes far beyond any organized religion (Cacioppe, 2000a; Klenke, 2003). In stark contrast, Hicks (2002) censured the notion that ‘spirituality unites, but religion divides’ and instead asserted that such an outlook does not accurately reflect their complex interrelationship. He contends that complying with spirituality as being antithetical to religion essentially neglects the existing tensions, ambiguities, and differences at the workplace (Hicks, 2002). He added that researchers who embrace the conception of bringing the ‘whole self’ to work have been inconsistent and should thereby reconsider their stance if they emphasize employees’ spirituality at work while disregarding their religious expressions (Hicks, 2002). Implications from Hicks (2002), Bandsuch and Cavanagh (2005) suggest that spirituality needs to be deliberated more diligently in a way that addresses and accommodates everyday religious expressions and diversity. Second, organization behavior scholars identified and expounded the following key spiritual values essential to instill spirituality in the workplace: integrity (Burack, 1999; Fairholm, 1996; Konz & Ryan, 1999; Neck & Milliman, 1994), fostering meaningful relationships (Neck & Milliman, 1994), focusing on well-being (Neck & Milliman, 1994), inner peace (Neck & Milliman, 1994), love (Burack, 1999; Fairholm, 1996; Neck & Milliman, 1994), truth (Neck & Milliman, 1994), right-conduct (Neck & Milliman, 1994), fairness (Burack, 1999; Fairholm, 1996), sense of service (Fairholm, 1996), and respecting others (Burack, 1999; Fairholm, 1996). Finally, researchers also drew upon the profound impact of embodying spirituality at individual and organizational levels. At an individual level, spirituality begets employees to experience higher levels of consciousness which eventually is reflected in their heightened intuitive faculties (Neck & Milliman, 1994; Vaughan, 1989). Intuition is regarded to be an essential managerial skill as it boosts both personal and organizational performance (Fairholm, 1996). When fuelled by a compelling organizational vision, spirituality-based intuition fosters creative expression and innovative thinking among employees (Bandsuch & Cavanagh, 2005; Neck & Milliman, 1994). Bierly et al. (2000) contend that spirituality is a key driver of wisdom through two rationales. First, the pursuit of wisdom entails critical self-reflection, experiential learning, and articulation of deeper goals. Essentially, spirituality facilitates wisdom by aiding individuals in formulating clear goals and objectives which are grounded in core universal values and a better, comprehensive understanding of their life’s purpose (Bierly et al., 2000). Second, wisdom goes beyond rational analysis and encompasses a deep sense of self-awareness, living with integrity, and abiding by truth. Wisdom embodies knowing the right thing from the wrong, thereby replacing individuals’ pursuit of their selfish interests with a sense of transcendence and togetherness. This implies that accruing wisdom is, by its very nature, a spiritual journey (Bierly et al., 2000). Through spirituality at the workplace, employees gain a strong sense of service, experience job satisfaction, personal growth and development (Bandsuch & Cavanagh, 2005; Fairholm, 1996; Hawley & Hawley, 1993; Konz & Ryan, 1999; Neck & Milliman, 1994). At an organizational level, spirituality fosters a sense of belongingness (Bandsuch & Cavanagh, 2005; Burack, 1999; Dent et al., 2005; Fairholm, 1996), employee loyalty and commitment (Bandsuch & Cavanagh, 2005; Neck & Milliman, 1994), superior workplace ethics and values (Bandsuch & Cavanagh, 2005; Cavanagh & Bandsuch, 2002), teamwork (Neck & Milliman, 1994), organizational learning (Bierly et al., 2000), and organizational performance (Bandsuch & Cavanagh, 2005; Klenke, 2003; Neck & Milliman, 1994).

Increasingly, there is a chorus of scholarly voices calling for workplace spirituality in organizations (Benefiel, 2005; Parameshwar, 2005; Smith & Rayment, 2007). Analyzing how organizations are still in their nascent stages of becoming more spiritual and examining the potential benefits or conflicts, it may engender (Howard, 2002), researchers from (Cluster 2) grapple with and critique the extant discourse on workplace spirituality. First, leadership scholars strived to outline the various dimensions and definitions of workplace spirituality. Ashmos and Duchon (2000) outlined workplace spirituality as ‘the recognition that employees have an inner life that nourishes and is nourished by meaningful work that takes place in the context of community’ (p.137). Furthermore, Giacalone and Jurkiewicz (2003) added that it ‘is a framework of organizational values evidenced in the culture that promotes employees’ experience of transcendence through the work process, facilitating their sense of being connected to others in a way that provided feelings of completeness and joy’ (p.13). Using a pragmatic approach, Smith and Rayment (2007) acknowledge that workplace spirituality is an expression of how organizations and the people within them envision work as a spiritual path offering opportunities for personal growth and contribution in meaningful ways for the greater societal good. They assert that workplace spirituality essentially echoes demonstrating care and concern, being compassionate and supportive of one another, just as it is about living with integrity and being honest with themselves and others (Smith & Rayment, 2007). Specifically, Smith and Rayment (2007) recapitulated workplace spirituality as an attempt through which both individuals and organizations strive to live out their core values more fully through their work. Although workplace spirituality may be defined in varied ways and its dimensions (for instance, compassion (see Gupta et al. (2014)), transcendence, and mindfulness (refer to Petchsawang and Duchon (2009))) are many, the following are the most important facets of it: (a) Inner life: It is the level of spirituality one possesses (Ashmos & Duchon, 2000; Gupta et al., 2014; Rozuel & Kakabadse, 2010). (b) Meaningful work: From an existentialist lens, researchers have contended that it is an innate need for human beings to seek meaning in whatever they do, and therefore, a sense of meaning and higher purpose that is aligned with people’s work is an essential part of human experience (Ashmos & Duchon, 2000; Houghton et al., 2016; Sukumarakurup & Christopher, 2002). The pursuit of meaningfulness in and at work cultivates a sense of joy that enables one to unleash their highest potential and be connected with things that they consider important in life (Ashmos & Duchon, 2000; Houghton et al., 2016). (c) Sense of community: Researchers attested that people seek belongingness and interconnectedness with one another as an expression of their spiritual selves through commitment, sharing, and mutual obligations, ultimately fostering authentic and meaningful relationships (Ashmos & Duchon, 2000; Gotsis & Kortezi, 2008; Houghton et al., 2016; Rozuel & Kakabadse, 2010). Second, researchers of workplace spirituality underscore a few challenges and dilemmas they may face while engaging in examining workplace spirituality. Benefiel (2005) and Lips-Wiersma (2000) succinctly pointed out one such paradox: Workplace spirituality: Should it only be considered worthwhile if it culminates in greater organizational outcomes? ‘On the one hand, spirituality, in its very essence, seeks to go beyond materialistic conceptions of meaning. On the other hand, … within the spirit at work field, there is a concern that if spirituality is not linked to materialistic outcomes for the organization, it may never be taken seriously within the world of work’ (Lips-Wiersma, 2000, p.13, 15). Along with the concern regarding the immanent contradiction of organizations reaping materialistic outcomes through workplace spirituality; the instrumentalistic purview of workplace spirituality (Gotsis & Kortezi, 2008; Smith & Rayment, 2007), organizational scholars also speculate if contemporary social science research techniques are able to encapsulate and measure the complex abstract nature of workplace spirituality in its entirety (Benefiel, 2005). Furthermore, organizational scholars also contemplate the Spirituality-Religion dichotomy (Gotsis & Kortezi, 2008; Houghton et al., 2016; Rozuel & Kakabadse, 2010; Smith & Rayment, 2007). Finally, leadership scholars conclude with the implications of workplace spirituality for leadership and organizations. To illustrate, Smith and Rayment (2007) posed eight key practical questions to help leaders appreciate why workplace spirituality is a need of the hour and how it should be embraced and nurtured. Additionally, they offered a global SMP fitness framework for guiding leaders to navigate through the potential complexities and challenges they might encounter while embodying workplace spirituality (Smith & Rayment, 2007). Moreover, within the realm of workplace spirituality, Pawar (2014) conducted an empirical study investigating the effects of leaders’ individual spirituality and organizational spirituality on their behavior (Leadership Spiritual Behaviors, henceforth, LSB) toward employees, and the findings revealed the significant direct effects of leaders’ individual and organizational spiritualities on LSB. Furthermore, Weinberg and Locander (2014) inquired about how leaders ensured workplace spirituality over time by employing it on an individual level. As a response, they offered a dyadic workplace spiritual mentoring approach wherein the emphasis is on developing an awareness of and nurturing the protégé’s inner life by catering to meaningful work that resonates with the protégé’s vocation, thus, facilitating a sense of transcendence through work (Weinberg & Locander, 2014). Additionally, organizational scholars explored how workplace spirituality facilitated organizational learning and transformation (Howard, 2002), considerably enhanced employees’ work attitudes (such as employees’ organizational commitment, job involvement, and satisfaction) (Pawar, 2009), reinforced trust (Rozuel & Kakabadse, 2010), and when infused with organizational ethics reaped superior organizational performance (Collins, 2010).

According to Fry (2003), the purview of discourses about spiritual leadership can be classified as being within the wider realm of workplace spirituality because there has been a significant overlap between motivation-based leadership theories and varied dimensions of workplace spirituality. Furthermore, he affirmed that any framework of spiritual leadership rooted in motivation theories must integrate and encompass aspects of workplace spirituality and spiritual survival. First, organizational leadership scholars in this cluster have outlined the core values, leadership traits, characteristics, and practices that embody an effective spiritual leader. To elaborate further, Whittington et al. (2005) leveraged biblical approaches to leadership for identifying and articulating the qualities essential for spiritual leaders by delving into the leadership attributes of Apostle Paul, as revealed in his first letter to the Thessalonians. Whittington et al. (2005) referred to Paul’s self-perpetuating leadership style as ‘Legacy leadership’ as it reflects the fact that not only Thessalonians but also churches all over were influenced by his leadership. These leadership scholars explicated that a spiritual leader’s qualities must be pure, affectionate, authentic, follower-centric, and sincere (Whittington et al., 2005). They further contended that a spiritual leader’s choice of methods should: reflect transparency and boldness in the face of opposition, be active and worthy of imitation, possess the ability to influence without exerting authority, and that the transformed lives of their followers should further reflect these principles (Whittington et al., 2005). On a similar note, Reave (2005) ascertained the key values and practices that must be embodied by a spiritual leader, and the focus of her study was to not impose spirituality upon the discourses of leadership literature but rather to distill from it any important elements that are iteratively emphasized in spiritual teachings. Reave (2005) further argued that it is imperative to study the confluence of spirituality and leadership because spiritual leaders fared better on measures of leadership effectiveness than their counterparts in other settings. According to Reave (2005), humility, integrity, and honesty are the critical spiritual values that determine the effectiveness of leadership. Furthermore, practices such as being respectful of others’ values, treating others fairly, expressing compassion and concern, listening attentively and responding to the needs of others, recognizing and appreciating others’ contributions, and engaging in reflective activities such as writing a journal, meditation and nature walks can further enhance leadership effectiveness (Reave, 2005). Additionally, Kriger and Seng (2005) highlighted the essential spiritual values such as humility, trust, forgiveness, gratitude, kindness, equanimity, inner peace, patience, empathy, integrity, inner joy, serving others, courage, and compassion that enhance leadership effectiveness. Second, within this cluster, researchers in the field of organizational leadership have attempted to conceptualize and construct a causal theory of spiritual leadership. For instance, L.W. Fry proposed the causal model of spiritual leadership on the basis of the intrinsic motivational model, which integrates and encompasses altruistic love, faith, vision, and theories of workplace spirituality. Furthermore, Fry et al. (2011) expounded that ‘spiritual leadership taps into organization members’ needs for transcendence and connection, to intrinsically motivate oneself and others and satisfy fundamental needs for spiritual well-being through calling and membership. Spiritual leadership emerges from the interaction of altruistic love, vision, and hope/faith in organizational members. The emergence of spiritual leadership then taps into the fundamental needs of both leaders and followers for their spiritual well-being through enhancing their sense of calling toward the unit and its goals and vision and a sense of membership with the group. Spiritual well-being (i.e., calling and membership) then serves to foster higher levels of organizational commitment, productivity, and performance’ (p.261). In the same vein, Kriger and Seng (2005) proposed a complex contingency theory of leadership by drawing upon inner values and worldviews implicitly shared by the following five major religions: Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, and Judaism. The rationale behind this study was to assert that underpinning each of the five major religious traditions of the world is a shared multi-level ontological approach to spiritual leadership, which can be employed at the organizational level to address the current organizational challenges (for instance, lack of meaning, purpose, and vision in and at work, corporate greed, increasing unethical practices, etc.). Following a similar course of thought, Fry and Kriger (2009) offered a foundational theory of being-centered leadership which integrates five ontological levels of being in order to lead effectively. Fry and Kriger (2009) maintained that leadership theories of the past often grappled with the notion that to lead effectively, a leader had to possess certain qualities (a state of ‘having’) or follow certain practices (a state of ‘doing’), but it was never about the state of ‘being.’ Through their study, Fry and Kriger (2009) sought to demonstrate how different levels of being (such as the sensible/physical word, images and imagination, soul, spirit, and non-duality) can offer varying contexts to facilitate a holistic understanding of effective leadership. Finally, most of the research papers within this cluster (8 out of 13) examined the relevance and significance of Fry’s (2003) causal theory of spiritual leadership in determining varied organizational outcomes. To illustrate further, Fry et al. (2005) tested the causal model of Spiritual Leadership Theory (SLT) based on longitudinal data gathered from the newly formed Apache Longbow helicopter attack squadron at Ft. Hood, Texas and the results of this investigation yielded positive correlations between the measures of spiritual leadership, spiritual survival/ spiritual wellbeing, organizational commitment and productivity, thus, validating the causal model of SLT in the context of army training and transformation. In another military academy setting, Fry et al. (2011) investigated how the causal model of SLT begets organizational commitment and performance at the unit level by gathering data from the cadets at the United States Military Academy. Furthermore, the causal model of SLT was offered as a paradigm for organizational transformation and for overcoming the detrimental effects of extended work-hour cultures by enhancing employees’ well-being and CSR without compromising the organization’s financial performance (Fry & Cohen, 2009). In addition to this, Fry et al. (2010) extended the ‘Spiritual Leadership Balanced Scorecard Business Framework,’ grounded in the nexus of new developments in strategic performance measurement and the causal model of SLT, as a potential catalyst for maximizing employees’ well-being, CSR and positive organizational outcomes including organizational productivity, organizational commitment, and organizational financial performance by significantly impacting the internal processes, output quality, and customer and stakeholder satisfaction. Using the sample drawn from the Baldrige Performance Excellence Program awardees, Fry et al. (2017) studied the impact of the causal model of SLT in determining performance excellence, and their findings corroborate the positive and significant effects of spiritual leadership on life satisfaction, work unit productivity and organizational commitment. Theorizing and extending the causal model of SLT theory (Fry, 2003) a step further, Chen and Li (2013) incorporated followers’ transcendental self-concepts in the causal model of SLT and asserted that spiritual leadership plays an integral role in heightening subordinates’ self-efficacy and self-esteem. Additionally, Chen and Li (2013) contended that cultural values moderate the effectiveness of spiritual leadership on organizational productivity and commitment, and in a Chinese cultural setting, their findings established that it is essential for the leaders of organizations to integrate and exercise spiritual leadership in addition to cultivating a healthy organizational climate which encourages employees to build their own positive self-concept, thus, reaping leadership effectiveness and positive organizational results.

In this domain (cluster), researchers study the impact of the interplay between spiritual leadership and workplace spirituality on individual and organizational outcomes. First, organizational scholars within this cluster shed light on how workplace spirituality reaps organizational performance and positive organizational behaviors. To elucidate further, Duchon and Plowman (2005) affirm that if a workplace acknowledges and supports employees’ inner lives by enabling them with meaningful work and fostering a sense of belongingness within the context of community, then it will be workplace spirituality that fuels organizational performance. On the same lines, pertaining to the context of primary healthcare organizations, Albuquerque et al. (2014) examined the impact of workplace spirituality on objective and perceived organizational performance and ascertained that workplace spirituality might assist organizational employees in effectuating new performance targets more quickly and effectively. Consequently, Duchon and Plowman (2005) emphasize the role spiritual leadership plays in modeling workplace spirituality by embracing a work environment of tolerance and freedom. In conclusion, they offer a theoretical model that explains how spiritual leadership engenders workplace spirituality which further enhances organizational performance. Organizational researchers also operationalized workplace spirituality alternatively as spiritual survival/ spiritual well-being addressing employees’ spiritual needs of calling and membership (Bayighomog & Araslı, 2019; Hunsaker, 2016). Chen and Yang (2012) argue that it is through spiritual leadership that employees experience meaningfulness at work and a sense of membership, leading to an environment where they feel appreciated and understood, further reinforcing organizational citizenship behavior. In their study, Chen and Yang (2012) explored the impact of spiritual leadership on organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) at an individual (altruism) and organizational level (conscientiousness) by performing a comparative analysis across industries of the sample drawn from retail and finance industries and found a positive correlation. Moreover, drawing upon the core virtues of Confucian philosophy, Hunsaker (2016) demonstrated how spiritual leadership was found to positively impact OCB on both an individual and organizational level. As a result, Hunsaker (2016) postulated that employees’ traditional Confucian mindset and a sense of calling and membership, operationalized as followers’ spiritual well-being, fully mediate the relationship between spiritual leadership and OCBs (Hunsaker, 2016). His research suggests, in summary, that spiritual leadership is significantly affected by core values and beliefs, such as Confucianism, in countries with deeply ingrained cultural customs and traditions. Following the same vein, Madison and Kellermanns (2013) investigated how spiritual well-being fully mediated the causal relationship between spiritual leadership and OCB in a family firm setting by contending that the essence of spiritual leadership is relationship-based, embracing both leaders’ principles and attending to followers’ needs of higher order, as is often true among family businesses, where a sense of belonging and calling is encouraged, and the results of their study revealed the same. Drawing insights from social identity and social exchange theories, Bayighomog and Araslı (2019) assessed the impact of spiritual leadership on employees’ customeroriented boundary-spanning behaviors (henceforth, COBSBs) that are operationalized through internal influence, service delivery, and external representation, referring to an aspect of customer-orientation management that taps into and cultivates the employees’ abilities to act in ways where employees go beyond their traditionally assigned work roles and connect the organization with its external stakeholders. The study findings from Bayighomog and Araslı (2019) corroborate the notion that spiritual leadership impacts employees’ COBSBs in a very positive and significant way and that causality is fully mediated by employees’ sense of spiritual survival and well-being.

First, researchers in this domain (cluster) drew synergies between spiritual leadership and other extant leadership paradigms. To illustrate further, transformational leadership encompasses the elements of ‘inspirational motivation’ and, therefore, can be correlated with spiritual leadership, given that even spiritual leaders must be inspiring and visionary while surpassing the pre-existing limitations (Crossman, 2010; Fairholm, 2003). According to Burns (1978), transformational leadership, like spiritual leadership, is inspirational in the sense that it entails elevating employees’ awareness of achieving organizational outcomes while intrinsically motivating them to transcend their self-interests for the holistic well-being of the organization (Sendjaya et al., 2008). In this manner, both spiritual leadership and transformational leadership invoke higher-order needs and aim at inspiring followers, as opposed to transactional leadership, which is characterized by mundane exchanges between the leaders and the led (Crossman, 2010). In similar lines of thought, servant leadership and spiritual leadership cross paths in many ways. For instance, Spears and Wagner-Marsh (1998, p.3) encapsulate servant leadership as ‘the leadership that emphasizes increased service to others, a holistic approach to work, promoting a sense of community, and the sharing of power in decision making. At its core, servant leadership is a long-term, transformational approach to life and work—in essence, a way of being—that has the potential for creating positive change throughout our society.’ Fry (2003, p.708) further adds that a servant leader ‘is attuned to spiritual values.’ It is intrinsically virtuous for both spiritual and servant leadership paradigms to nurture within the workplace a sense of empathy, vision, hope, humility, integrity, love, meaning, respect, and interconnectedness (Fry, 2003; Spears, 2004). Sendjaya et al. (2008) asserted that servant leadership, too, is deeply ingrained in vision, hope, and faith and that both spiritual and servant leaders strive to facilitate a sense of purpose, meaning, and belongingness in the workplace by intrinsically motivating oneself and others, abiding by virtuous leadership practices, and engaging in service to the greater good and expression of gratitude to the higher power. The notion of serving the greater societal good also embodies demonstrating concern for the environment. Accordingly, there has been deliberation in the managerial literature regarding the synergy between spiritual leadership and environmental leadership. Raelin (2003) argues that spiritual leaders must be environmentally responsible and play their part in creating a greener, more sustainable world. He believes that when spiritual leaders contribute to a greener planet, they are in a balanced way, serving the spiritual and environmental aspects of the ‘common good’ (Raelin, 2003). Crossman (2010, 2011) drew strong parallels between environmental and spiritual leadership by affirming that spirituality and environment are innate aspects of the human psyche and contends that native indigenous cultures often emphasized the harmonious interwoven relationship between nature and the spirit. He further asserts that both the spiritual and environmental leadership works of literature highlight the role of a leader to be compassionate and hold a profound relationship with self and nature (Crossman, 2010, 2011). Finally, within this domain (cluster), researchers elaborate upon several forms of leadership that are rooted in spirituality. Karakas and Sarigollu (2012, 2013) maintain that an increasing lack of confidence in leadership has led to disenchantment with leadership, as evidenced by unbridled greed, layoffs, and immoral and unethical scandals. Moreover, they acknowledge a growing sense of uncertainty and flux in the contemporary business world owing to the advent of globalization and technological advancements. In light of the aforementioned concerns, they called for a leadership paradigm based on the ‘common good.’ They inductively drew upon positive organizational scholarship and proposed the concept of benevolent leadership grounded in spirituality, morality, community responsiveness, and vitality. Karakas and Sarigollu (2013) distinguished benevolent leadership from other value-based leadership paradigms by elucidating that (a) It is explicitly geared toward bringing positive change to human systems, (b) By encompassing spirituality, vitality, community responsiveness, and morality, benevolent leadership addresses ethical, social, transformational, and spiritual concerns, (c) Through benevolent leadership, leaders can establish compassionate and virtuous organizations. In a similar vein of thought, Wang and Hackett (2016) drew on philosophical standpoints of Confucianism and Aristotelianism and proffered the concept of virtuous leadership. According to Wang and Hackett (2016), virtuous leaders possess these cardinal virtues: They are courageous, humane, truthful, and prudent, have temperament, and exercise justice, thus, fostering an ethical climate in their organizations (Wang & Hackett, 2016). As a part of their study, they also sought to establish the distinctiveness of virtuous leadership from other value-laden leadership paradigms by affirming that ‘values can be held but not practiced but virtues are sustained only through practice’ (Wang & Hackett, 2016) (See Fig. 4).
